title: Which Room Is the Meeting In?
prerequisites: Recognise room names, floor numbers, and clock times.
observable_outcome: The learner asks politely for a missing meeting-room detail, then confirms the room and floor in one checking question.
learning_objective: Clarify which meeting room to use, then confirm the floor and room accurately.

scenario.setting: An office reception desk before a client meeting.
scenario.prompt: Your invitation says Client check-in at 10:00 on the third floor. The room name is smudged. Reception says the meeting is in the Orchid Room.
scenario.puzzle: Which clue is missing, and how can you ask for it politely before checking the full location?
scenario.privacy_note: The company, meeting, and room names are fictional teaching data.

model.clarify: Could you tell me which room the meeting is in, please?
model.customer_reply: The Orchid Room, on the third floor.
model.confirm: So that's the Orchid Room on the third floor, right?
model.neutral_variant: Which room is the meeting in, please?

language_focus.grammar: After Could you tell me, use statement order in the embedded question: which room the meeting is in. Do not repeat direct-question order as which room is the meeting in.
language_focus.meaning: The floor narrows the location, but the room name identifies the exact meeting place. The readback joins both details for confirmation.
language_focus.appropriateness: Could you tell me ... please? is polite at a reception desk. Which room is the meeting in, please? is also correct and more direct. Which room, please? works when the situation is already clear.
language_focus.location_language: Use in for the room and on for the floor: in the Orchid Room, on the third floor.

choice_activity.prompt: The time and floor are clear. Which detail still needs clarification?

options.feedback: Correct. The exact room is missing, so ask which room the meeting is in.
The invitation clearly says 10:00. Asking again would not solve the missing-room problem.
The third floor is already clear. You still need the room name.

request_activity.prompt: Choose a correct, polite reception question.

options.text: Could you tell me which room the meeting is in, please?
options.feedback: Correct. The polite frame is followed by statement order: the meeting is in.

options.text: Which room is the meeting in, please?
options.feedback: Also correct. This direct question is polite with please, though less indirect.

options.text: Could you tell me which room is the meeting in?
options.feedback: The meaning is understandable, but standard embedded-question order is which room the meeting is in.

slot_activity.prompt: Match each clue to its meeting-location slot.

feedback.time: Correct. 10:00 tells you when the meeting starts.
feedback.floor: 10:00 is a clock time, not a floor.

feedback.time: Third floor tells you where in the building, not when.
feedback.floor: Correct. Third floor narrows the building location.
feedback.room: This is a floor, not the exact room.

feedback.time: Orchid Room is a place, not a time.
feedback.floor: Orchid Room names the exact room, not the floor.
feedback.room: Correct. Orchid Room is the exact meeting place.

production_task.scenario: A workshop starts at 14:30 on the second floor. The room name is unclear. Reception says Palm Room.
production_task.instruction: Write one polite clarification question. Then write one complete readback question with Palm Room and the second floor.
acceptable_responses: Could you tell me which room the workshop is in, please? So that's the Palm Room on the second floor, right?
Which room is the workshop in, please? Let me check: the Palm Room on the second floor. Is that correct?
rubric: I asked for the missing room.
I repeated the room and floor.
production_task.valid_variants: Both direct and embedded questions can work. Meeting, workshop, session, and event are acceptable when they fit the situation.

review_prompt: Tomorrow, explain why we say Could you tell me which room the meeting is in? rather than Could you tell me which room is the meeting in?

scenes.title: Read the invitation
scenes.caption: Client check-in: 10:00, third floor, room name unclear.
scenes.explanation: The office opens in layers while the invitation slides forward. The time and floor are readable, but the room strip stays covered.

scenes.title: Spot the missing clue
scenes.caption: 10:00 is clear. Third floor is clear. The room name is missing.
scenes.explanation: The known time and floor tiles lock into place. A labelled room-shaped gap remains open.

scenes.title: Ask politely
scenes.caption: Could you tell me which room the meeting is in, please?
scenes.explanation: The visitor pivots toward reception. A three-layer speech card unfolds to show the polite frame and embedded question.

scenes.title: Keep statement order
scenes.caption: Could you tell me + which room + the meeting is in?
scenes.explanation: Word tiles reorder after the polite frame. The subject the meeting stays before is.

scenes.title: Confirm both clues
scenes.caption: So that's the Orchid Room on the third floor, right?
scenes.explanation: The third-floor tile and Orchid Room plaque stack into one route card. A check mark pivots into view.

scenes.title: Your workshop
scenes.caption: Palm Room, second floor, 14:30.
scenes.explanation: A visitor moves to a new floor. Ask for the room, then read back Palm Room and the second floor.

visual.title: Find the missing room, then confirm the route
visual.alt_text: A layered papercut office route. Known time and floor clues lead to a polite room question. The answer adds the Orchid Room, then room and floor combine in one confirmation.
visual.prose: First separate the known clues from the missing clue. Ask which room using a direct or embedded question. In the embedded version, keep statement order: the meeting is in. Then repeat the room and floor together and invite confirmation.
